A system of equations has infinitely many solutions when both equations represent the same line. This occurs when both equations have the same slope and the same [MATH: y]-intercept.

In other words, the two equations represent the same line if one equation is a constant multiple of the other.

First, we observe that the left-hand side of the second equation appears to be a multiple of the left-hand side of the first equation. To see this, let’s multiply the first equation by [MATH: 3{:}]

[MATH: 3(− 2x + 9y)|= 3(7); − 6x + 27y|= 21]

Thus, for the system to have infinitely many solutions, the second equation must be identical to [MATH: -6x + 27y = 21.]

Therefore, the constant [MATH: k] must be

[MATH: k = 21.]

sections.normalized_html:
A system of equations has infinitely many solutions when both equations represent the same line. This occurs when both equations have the same slope and the same [MATH: y]-intercept.

In other words, the two equations represent the same line if one equation is a constant multiple of the other.

We start by eliminating fractions from the first equation to make comparison easier.

We multiply both sides of the first equation by [MATH: 24] (the least common multiple of [MATH: 6] and [MATH: 8]):

[MATH: 24((5)/(6)x − (1)/(8)y)|= 24(3); 20x − 3y|= 72]

So the system becomes

[MATH: {20x − 3y = 72; rx − 9y = s]

Now, if one equation is a constant multiple of the other, all coefficients and constants are proportional. That means

[MATH: \frac{r}{20} = \frac{(-9)}{(-3)} = \frac{s}{72}.]

To find the value of [MATH: r,] we focus on the proportion

[MATH: \frac{r}{20}= \frac{(-9)}{(-3)} = 3.]

Therefore, multiplying both sides by [MATH: 20,] we find that the value of [MATH: r] is

[MATH: r = 3 \cdot 20 = 60.]

sections.normalized_html:
One of the equations in a system of linear equations is [MATH: y = -5x - 4.] The system has infinitely many solutions. Which equation could be the second equation in this system?

  1. [MATH: 4y = 4(-5x - 4)]

  2. [MATH: 4y = 4(-5x) - 4]

III . [MATH: 4y = -5x + 4(-4)]
sections.readable_text:
One of the equations in a system of linear equations is [MATH: y = -5x - 4.] The system has infinitely many solutions. Which equation could be the second equation in this system?

1. [MATH: 4y = 4(-5x - 4)]
2. [MATH: 4y = 4(-5x) - 4]

III . [MATH: 4y = -5x + 4(-4)]

sections.normalized_html:
A system of equations has infinitely many solutions when both equations represent the same line. This occurs when both equations have the same slope and the same [MATH: y]-intercept.

In other words, the two equations represent the same line if one equation is a constant multiple of the other.

We are given that one equation in the system is [MATH: y = -5x - 4.]

Now, we want to find another equation among the choices that is a constant multiple of this one.

We reject [MATH: y = 4(-5x - 4)] and [MATH: y = 4(-5x) - 4] because they have the same left-hand side as our equation but different right-hand sides.

Note that the remaining choices all have [MATH: 4y] on the left-hand side.

We get [MATH: 4y] on the left-hand side of our equation if we multiply both sides of [MATH: y = -5x - 4] by [MATH: 4.] This gives the equivalent equation:

[MATH: 4y = 4(-5x - 4)]

Compare this with the choices that have [MATH: 4y] on the left-hand side:

  • [MATH: 4y = 4(-5x - 4) \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}]

  • [MATH: 4y = 4(-5x) - 4 \quad {\color{red}\times}]

  • [MATH: 4y = -5x + 4(-4) \quad {\color{red}\times}]

Therefore, among the choices, [MATH: 4y = 4(-5x - 4)] is a constant multiple of [MATH: y = -5x - 4.]

Therefore, I could be the second equation in the system.

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A system of equations has infinitely many solutions when both equations represent the same line. This occurs when both equations have the same slope and the same [MATH: y]-intercept.

In other words, the two equations represent the same line if one equation is a constant multiple of the other.

First, we observe that the left-hand side of the second equation appears to be a multiple of the left-hand side of the first equation. To see this, let’s multiply the first equation by [MATH: 3{:}]

[MATH: 3(− 2x + 9y)|= 3(7); − 6x + 27y|= 21]

Thus, for the system to have infinitely many solutions, the second equation must be identical to [MATH: -6x + 27y = 21.]

Therefore, the constant [MATH: k] must be

[MATH: k = 21.]
